title: Alphabet Poems (Acrostics)
lead: Some Hebrew poems begin each line or stanza with the next letter of the 22-letter alphabet, from alef to tav. Nine psalms, the poem on the capable wife in Proverbs 31, four chapters of Lamentations and part of Nahum 1 are built this way, and English translations can show it only in notes and headings.

sections.h: The alphabet poems of the Bible
sections.b: Hebrew alphabet poems take several shapes. One line per letter: Psalms 25, 34 and 145, Proverbs 31:10–31, and Lamentations 1, 2 and 4. Half a line per letter: Psalms 111 and 112. Two verses per letter, roughly: Psalm 37 and the broken alphabet of Psalms 9–10, which runs across both psalms. Three verses per letter: Lamentations 3 (66 verses). Eight verses per letter: Psalm 119 (176 verses). Nahum 1:2–8 has a partial alphabet. Lamentations 5 has 22 verses but no alphabet. Several poems bend the pattern: Lamentations 2, 3 and 4 put pe before ayin, Psalms 25 and 34 add a closing verse that begins with pe, and Psalm 145 lacks a nun line in the Hebrew (see the variant at Psalm 145:13). A Hebrew alphabet poem on wisdom closes Sirach (Sirach 51:13–30) and survives in the Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran.

sections.b: Scholars give four reasons, which can overlap. Alphabets help memory, like a numbered list. They express completeness: the whole subject "from A to Z", whether praise (Psalm 145), grief (Lamentations) or love of God's law (Psalm 119). They show craft and order, a poem shaped with care. And they were school exercises: practice alphabets (abecedaries) scratched on pottery have been found in Israel, at Izbet Sartah and Tel Zayit. Acrostics are older than Israel: a Babylonian poem known as the Babylonian Theodicy spells out a sentence with the first signs of its stanzas, naming its author.
